/parashas-mikeitz-dec-3rd-4th-2021/: There is a rhythm to life. We breath in and then out. We step with our right foot, and then with our left. We sleep and then we awake. We see for a moment, but then we blink.

Our Sages stated thousands of years ago that the world is not a stagnant, fixed reality as it appears but that HaShem literally recreates the physical universe at every single moment. Recently, quantum physics has corroborated this ancient teaching, revealing that the entire world is popping into and out of existence at each instant, like the blink of an eye!
Our Sages also teach that man is called an “Olam Katan”, a small world. Therefore, in some very profound way, we are also bursting into and out of existence.

Until the wellsprings of the Ba’al Shem Tov began to spread forth, our understanding of this reality remained obscure. However, the Ba’al Shem Tov and the great Chassidic Masters dug down deep and pulled out the most potent parallel between the pulsating nature of man’s consciousness and the pulsating rhythm of the world.

Chassidus explains that man’s mind is in a constant state of fluctuation between expansion and constriction. The source for the ups and downs of life comes from an inner psycho-spiritual dynamic known as “Ratzo v’Shov”, running and returning. In the famous sixth lesson of
, Rebbe Nachman utilizes his powerful understanding of “Ratzo v’Shov”, to shed light on the bipolar state of man and the key to attaining harmony with the natural ebbs and flows of our mind.
At times Rebbe Nachman explains that we will be feeling particularly good. We will have tranquility of mind. Our emotional state will be joyful. Our actions constructive.

This is coming from an expanded state of consciousness known as Mochin D’Gadlut. Then in one instant, our thoughts become dark, our emotions turbulent, and our actions destructive. This iscoming from a constricted state of consciousness known Mochind’Katnut.

In the modern world, we seek psychotherapy for this pattern. However, Rebbe Nachman explains that the problem is not in the pattern itself, but how we respond to it. Put simply, in times of expanded consciousness, our orientation to life should be growth oriented and explorative, with an intense desire to achieve a greater truth than the one we currently possess. The focus being on climbing from rung to rung.

On the other hand, when constricted consciousness strikes, we should not continue our quest for understanding and truth seeking. Instead, we should empty our minds completely of what we hold to be true, and simply believe that what is taking place is for the very best. The focus being on not getting pushed off the rung completely.
One might scoff at such a response as being ignorant and naïve. However, the depths of this teaching runs very deep.

How does one actually achieve greater understanding? Rebbe Nachman is telling us that when trouble strikes, your ability to “know” is purposefully concealed from you by HaShem. At this point your choice is either to resist, as we so often do, or to believe more deeply. Once one’s belief and hope deepens, his or her capacity to experience a higher truth paradoxically expands along with it. When approached correctly, the constriction of “knowing” paves the way for greater understanding.

In this week’s Parashah, Yosef ends his twenty two year long period of intense servitude and begins to become the most influential and fruitful figure in the world. While this transition might appear to be highly incongruent, it is actually Yosef’s positive response to negative circumstances that created the possibility for this sweeping transformation.

Our Sages teach us that while in prison, Yosef was a “jumping man”. Yosef had accustomed himself to respond to his problems with dancing and singing. He did not attempt to understand the “unfortunate” circumstances of his life. Instead, he decided to face them with the utmost faith and joy. As a result, he was able to see the good in his life, and achieve greater clarity than those around him. It was with this intense clarity, that he left prison and became viceroy of the most powerful country in the world.
Rebbe Nachman teaches that only a person who becomes expert in going up and down, can truly find his way back to HaShem, and bring everyone along with him.
Yosef’s ability to go up and down successfully ultimately led to his own personal redemption as well as that of everyone around him.

May HaShem bless us to know how to run and return like Yosef HaTzaddik, facing our challenges with strength, simplicity, and joy, and responding to our successes with an ever growing yearning for greater understanding and clarity. With this, we will find our way back to the One who loves us so dearly and waits longingly for our true arrival.

/parashas-mishpatim-jan-29nd-2022/: The End is Wedged in the Beginning

In any completed process, there are two main components. These components are not at all the same, but they are undoubtedly equal. The first component is the beginning, and this reflects unlimited potential. The second component is the end, reflected by actualized reality (
According to Kabbalah, the beginning of any process is rooted in the spiritual quality of “Zachar,” maleness. The finality of any process is rooted in the spiritual quality of “Nekeva,” femaleness (
). And just as the beginning lacks meaning without the end, so too the end does not take effect without the beginning.

From here we can extract a basic principle of the Torah. Men and women are unequivocally equal. Despite superficial perception to the contrary, the intrinsic differences associated with both masculinity and femininity from the perspective of the Torah do not in any way undermine their deep rooted equality. In fact, their inherent differences actually serve to enhance, perfect, and complete the properties of the other. The Sages elucidate this point explicitly.
Commenting on the first verse in this week’s Torah Portion, “And these are the laws that you must place before them” (
), our Sages taught: The words “before them” indicate that in regard to all Torah laws, woman is equated with man (
). And while this is certainly referring to men and women in the simple sense, “man” and “woman” can also refer to two different types of essential spiritual service.
“Man” corresponds to the intensive learning of Torah and “Woman” corresponds to authentic Tefillah, heartfelt prayer (

). Rebbe Nachman teaches that as long as we do not make a balanced space for the existence of both forms of service in our own lives, than our individual and collective redemption will continue to allude us (
). This is the secret of the halachah in the Shulchan Aruch which states that it is good for a person pray in the same place that he learns (Shulchan Aruch, (90:18).

Over my half decade of teaching Torah, I have noticed the lack of harmony between these two essential elements in almost ever person I encounter. One person spends the majority of his day learning Torah, but privately feels very far from an authentic relationship with the One who created him- for “It is not good for man to be alone” (

). Another person spends countless hours in secluded meditation in the field pouring his heart out to HaShem Mitberach, but finds that he lacks true clarity and understanding. For the female dimension, Tefillah, “has no light of her own” (

It personally took me quite some time to allow myself the permission to give equal time and energy into both. When I first became Ba’al Teshuva, I immersed myself in learning everything I could find, but did not actually experience HaShem in my life in a palpable way. I transitioned to speaking to HaShem at every chance I could get in Hitbodedut, but ultimately found that I came out feeling even more confused and heavier than when I began.
The reason is very simple. Torah and Tefillah are both equal, and most importantly, synergetic (
). Rebbe Nachman explains that it is the Torah that one learns that allows his Tefillot to get answered (
). On the other hand, it is Tefillah which nurtures and waters one’s Torah learning, allowing one to achieve ever increasing levels of G-d consciousness (

Torah and Tefillah are not two separate entities living in a vacuum. They are two sides to a double edged sword, and it only with this fully loaded weapon that one can overcome all the challenges one has to face in this world, while simultaneously achieving the greatest level of closeness to HaShem (

I highly encourage anyone reading this to honestly assess the unspoken value they have placed on either Torah learning or heartfelt Tefillah in their lives. If you find that over the course of time, you have marginalized one of these practices for the sake of the other, then reassess. Because men and women were created equal. And without making a legitimate effort to equalize these two powerful forces in one’s life, the possibility for leaving one’s personal exile will always remain elusive.
The Rebbe concluded, “The Mitnagdim argue that Torah study is a Jew’s main devotion. The Chassidim argue that prayer is the main devotion. But I say “Pray, learn, pray” (

Reb Noson shares with us important insights into avodas Hashem based on a pasuk found in this week’s parashah. The pasuk reads as follows: “When you lend money to My people, to the poor person [who is] with you, you shall not behave toward him as a lender; you shall not impose interest upon him.…” (22:24, translation from Chabad.org).

Reb Noson offers a novel reading of this pasuk by demonstrating that the pasuk is also referring to the way Hashem relates to the Jewish people. He explains how, in truth, it would be fitting for Hashem to return the world to “tohu v’vohu” given our many sins. Nevertheless, Hashem sustains us only with His chesed in the aspect of a “loan,” where Hashem does not exact payment from us immediately, but rather is constantly extending the “deadline” of payment in order that we return and pay Hashem for the debts we owe through the sins we have committed.

What emerges from Reb Noson’s understanding of the text are ideas that can energize and transform the way in which we approach our service of G-d. First and foremost, Reb Noson encourages us to see every moment of our lives, not as a right, but rather as a debt that we owe Hashem.
As Rav Shlomo Wolbe eludicates in

, where he describes how every person needs to consider – how am I obligated to conduct myself in each moment? The attitude is one of perceiving responsibility as the essential mode of experience, rather than entitlement. Therefore, an important shift in mindset occurs when a person understands that nothing is truly a given in his or her life. On the contract, every movement, every gesture, every breath is a gift from Above.
What are these “debts” that we owe Hashem? Reb Noson makes it a point to convey that our “debts” specifically come out of our sins. Rabbi Chaim Miller, in his translation and elucidation of

, explains that “evil… means a blocking of G-d consciousness” (p. 94). In other words, when a person sins, he or she is committing an act – either in thought, word, or action – that severs oneself from awareness of the Divine, ultimately leading to some form of fallenness.

Perhaps, then, one understanding of the repayment of the debt is a person’s ability to re-anchor oneself within G-d consciousness. Said differently, one’s responsibility to the moment is to energize the moment with the awareness that this experience comes directly from Hashem. In so doing, we “upgrade our consciousness” as my teacher, Rav Gerzi, so often explains and return those “fallen sparks” to their Source.

However, there is a further point. Reb Noson writes that Hashem is constantly extending the deadline of payment. Why? Ultimately, because Hashem believes in our ability to pay back our debts. Hashem believes in our ability to believe in Him. As we say everyday in davening, Hashem “maintains His faith to those asleep in the dust” (Artscroll translation).

No doubt, in these final moments before Mashiach, we are marred by the dirt of this world. Nevertheless, Hashem has emunah in our capacity to wipe the dust from our eyes and see how everything is truly from Him.

/parashas-shemos-dec-24th-25th-2021/: The Torah is not a history book. Its not even a religious doctrine. The Torah is the essential psycho-spiritual guide to inner transformation. No where is that more evident than in the second of the five books of the Torah which we are beginning this Shabbos,

Parshat Shemot is a stunningly comprehensive treatise on the exile of one’s true self. How does one become lost in life? What events take place along the way that deepen the loss of one’s essential self over time? Why does a person have to grapple with exile in the first place? And finally, what’s the catalyst that pushes one to ultimately find him or herself? All of these questions are thoroughly examined in
The answer to all of these questions are to be found in the seventh lesson of

. There, Rebbe Nachman concludes that the cause of all personal and collective exile begins and ends with two haunting words, “chesron b’emunah,” a lack of faith. It is the lack of conviction in one’s core beliefs that cause him or her to be exiled. Nothing more, nothing less.

Rebbe Nachman was once presenting a powerful discourse on the root cause of heaviness in one’s daily life. Rebbe Nachman concluded that to the degree that one lacks belief, to that degree everything in his life feels heavy.

In hearing this, Rav Natan, the main disciple of Rebbe Nachman, became visibly upset. Contemplating the heaviness of his own life and the inordinate difficulty with which each task in his day required, Rav Natan blurted out in pain and confusion, “But if there is one thing I have, it is faith!” His Rebbe responded, “It is true. You believe in HaShem. But you do not believe in yourself.”

The exile has never been more palpable or our lives more heavy than they are right now. Rebbe Nachman predicted this explicitly over two hundred years ago. But we must understand that the way we came in is the same way we must go out. Exile began with a lack of belief. Redemption will begin with a blossoming of belief. And no belief is more fundamental to our generation than the belief in one’s self.

I remember a very intense session of Hitbodedut I had while living in New York a few years ago. I had put away my smart phone along with all other possible distractions and entered the field. Feeling the heaviness of life, I poured my heart out to HaShem. As I was reaching the end of my daily, hour-long conversation with HaShem, I came to a startling realization. My emotional pain was not coming from those around me. It was not even coming from the intense challenges I had been presented with in my life. It was all due to the fact that I did not really believe in myself.

Ever since I had this epiphany, a day has not gone by that I have not prayed to HaShem to be able to truly believe in myself. That I am good. That I am capable. That I have the strength to rise above my inherent lackings. That I have a mission in this world that is real and meaningful, and that I must pursue it at all costs. As a result of this daily effort, I have felt a degree of freedom even before redemption has truly arrived.

I bless each of us to be able to take Rebbe Nachman’s most emphatic advice. To take a time alone each day to cultivate one’s belief in HaShem. One’s belief in His Torah. One’s belief in True Tzaddikim. And perhaps most importantly, the belief in one’s self.

/parashas-terumah-feb-5th-29nd-2022/: There is a beautiful moment in Torah סה where Rebbe Nachman describes the existence of a supernal field. And, in this field, the most gorgeous trees and vegetation grow. So much so, that the Rebbe says that it is impossible to describe the beauty of this field. He explains that the trees and vegetation are really the holy souls of the Jewish people. As Rabbi Chaim Kramer elucidates in the English commentary to this Torah, this supernal field is the expression of the Shechinah Itself (

However, there are many “naked souls” who roam outside the perimeter of this field. These souls, in their spiritual impoverishment, are not allowed to enter and their deepest yearning is to return to the .שדה

The above synopsis is only a glimpse into the first section of a profound Torah with many facets to it. And, in truth, my words are coarse in comparison to the beauty that exists on those pages in sefer
Nonetheless, it is with this introduction, I would like to begin.

When I heard Rav Moshe Weinberger share this Torah, I believe he characterized the field that Rebbe Nachman talks about as Hashem’s garden. How often do we feel like those naked souls wandering outside Hashem’s garden?

Our trail through life can feel thick with brush and, as we trudge forward, contending with the realities of our physical existence, our eyes grow weary. In our weariness, the Echad that we declare everyday becomes blurry and we descend into the fragmented shards of our lives, confused and in pain.
How can we get back to this garden? How can we return to the Echad? Of course, Rebbe Nachman presents a paradigm shifting answer in the Torah itself.
Indeed, I would like to offer an insight that is in harmony with the tzaddik’s explanation, but through the lens of this week’s parashah.

Parashas Terumah begins, “Hashem spoke to Moshe: Speak to the Children of Israel and let them take for Me a donation, from every man whose heart motivates him you shall take My donation” (25:1-2). The Torah continues and proceeds to list out the different materials that can be donated for the construction of the Mishkan. Then, in verse eight, the Torah famously writes, “They shall make a Sanctuary for Me so that I may dwell among them.”

We know that, on the level of penimiyus, the construction of the physical Mishkan can be compared to the construction of the spiritual Mishkan that exists within the privacy of our own inner worlds. And I hearken back to the words of Rav Weinberger on Tisha B’Av two years ago when he describes how is it possible to raise up our hearts to Hashem when our hearts have become as hard as stone? And, based on a moshel that Rebbe Nachman gives, Rav Weinberger explains that the only way to offer a heart of stone to Hashem is to take a hammer and smash the heart into pieces. Now, with trembling hands, we can lift up those shards to Hashem Himself.
What is the gold, silver, and copper of my inner world? What is the turquoise, purple, and scarlet wool of the heart? What are the materials of my internality that I am offering to Hashem?
I would like to propose the materials of the inner Mishkan, so to speak, are the shards of that broken heart.

When a person closes the door of his closet and sits in the darkness with his back bent over and says in hisbodedus, “Hashem, here it is: my pain and my humanity, my good and my bad, my love and my fear, my tears
and my laughs – I offer them up to You. Every ripple of my life comes from You and even though I intellectually know that to be true, help me to feel that truth in my heart.”

And, it is through the shaking voice of a Jew searching for his Creator, seeking the Echad in his life, that the heart begins to break. With those very rubbles, then “[t]hey shall make a Sanctuary for Me…”
My dear friends, with the help of the Almighty, may we speak to Hashem in truth and enter the garden again with the terumah of our broken hearts.
/parashas-tetzaveh-feb-12th-2022/: In the beginning of Parashat Tetzaveh, HaShem instructs Moshe to encourage the Jewish People to bring to him “pure, pressed olive oil for lighting” (Shemot 27:20). All the pristine oil that Moshe gathered would then be used to illuminate the Menorah in the form of a “ner tamid,” a perpetual lighting. This unique luminary in the Mishkan would serve as the model and prototype for the beacon of light which would shine forth from the Beit HaMikdash to the entire world (Menachot 86B).

Paradoxically, the process of unearthing this potent, ethereal light begins with tremendous pressure and weight placed on the physical olives themselves. Through intense duress alone, the olives then give birth to a wondrous oil capable of brilliant illumination.

This entire paradigm alludes to the deep, internal process of a Jewish person drawing out the inner light stored within him or herself in order to provide illumination for those all around, and in turn, becoming a “light unto the nations” (Yeshaya 49:6). The goal and destination of a Jew is certainly wondrous, but the path to lighting up one’s brethren is nonetheless preceded by an intense experience of being “katit,” crushed.

As Chazal famously teach, “Why are the Jews compared to olives? The olive sits upon its branch. It is plucked, squeezed, ground, and crushed, and only then does it give its oil. So too, when the Jews endure suffering, they show their mettle” (Shemot Rabbat 36:1). What allows a person the strength and inner fortitude to endure such intense trials and tribulations on their journey to fulfilling their unique potential?

In my favorite lesson of Likutey Moharan known in Breslov circles as “The Rebbe’s Letter,” Rebbe Nachman unusually and quite forwardly addresses his students, both in the present and to us now in the future, in the first person. The lesson is reminiscent of a letter written to a dear friend. Here, Rebbe Nachman exhorts each and every one of us in our uniquely challenging path towards actualizing one’s innermost self with these potent words, “When a person begins serving HaShem, the way is that they show him rejection. It seems as if HaShem is completely ignoring him and not turning to him at all because HaShem does not want him at all.

A person needs to be very stubborn, encouraging himself very, very much and paying no attention whatsoever to all this, for in truth, all distancing is nothing but being brought near. A person needs tremendous determination to be strong and courageous, to hold on and maintain his position even if they cause him to fall time and again. This is because one must surely experience all these falls, descents, confusions, and so on before entering the gates of holiness. The True Tzaddikim underwent all this. And so we heard from a True Tzaddik who said: “Had anyone, no matter whom, told me when I first began serving HaShem: “Brother! Be strong and hold on!” I would have run very quick in serving HaShem. For (that Tzaddik) too, experienced all the aforementioned, yet did not hear any encouragement, from anybody. Remember this well! Give yourself much encouragement, and do what you can in serving HaShem. Then, with the accruement of days and years, with HaShem’s help, you will surely enter into the gates of holiness. For HaShem is full of compassion and wants you very much. And so the rule my beloved brother, is to be very strong and courageous” (Likutey Moharan Tinyana, 48).

The True Tzaddik whom Rebbe Nachman is mysteriously alluding to appears to be himself. But the open ended nature of Rebbe Nachman’s disclaimer lends itself to interpreting these very words to ourselves as well. This is supported by the fact that Rebbe Nachman strongly asserted that anyone who had the courage to be his faithful disciple, without veering even the slightest bit from his established path, would become a great Tzaddik in his own right, come what may (Chayei Moharan, 320).

Over the course of my years since becoming Ba’al Teshuva and, with HaShem’s compassion, ultimately finding the Rebbe who so deeply resonated with the root of my soul, I have repeatedly drawn tremendous encouragement and inspiration from this letter. Continuously overcoming debilitating mental health conditions and psycho-spiritual vulnerabilities in order to provide light to my family and friends around me has proven to be the most formidable task of my life. And yet, the oil which has been produced by the constant “crushing,” has become a blazing fire of hope and consolation for those around me. This is my pride and joy in both this world and the next. All of this is in merit of my “Moshe Rabbeinu,” the Tzaddik Yesod Olam, Rebbe Nachman, from whom all this oil has been excavated by and gathered to.

I know I have stated this many times. But I will continue to do so, because this point requires constant encouragement. Do not ever give up. If you fall down, force yourself with whatever means necessary to dust yourself off and get back up again. Even if you fall many times throughout a day, find the courage to start over again. And even if you feel that you are alone in your struggles, you must know that I am over here fighting the very same fight with you.

And remember, each time you force yourself to begin anew, you are drawing out more and more pure oil. It is this sacred oil which will serve as the primary source of light in the final Beit HaMikdash, a brilliant luminance which will light up the whole world. A real and everlasting “ner tamid.” In the meantime, my dear brother, hold on.

When Rebbe Nachman was thirty years old, he moved to the city of Breslov. It was there that he attracted a large number of students and disciples. However, as his Chassidim came to understand fairly quickly, to have any type of relationship with Rebbe Nachman came with tremendous resistance. The closer the relationship to the Rebbe, the greater the resistance. The greatest of which came from the vehement opposition of Rebbe Nachman’s very own peers.

The Baal Shem Tov, Rebbe Nachman’s great-grandfather and the forebear of Chassidus, drew enmity from those who didn’t have the merit to taste the sweetness of his novel approach to experiencing genuine closeness with HaShem. These enemies

are historically known as “Mitnagdim,” opposers of the Baal Shem Tov and Chassidus in general. While this would be enough of a challenge for any future Chassid to contend with, Rebbe Nachman drew the ire not only of the “Mitnagdim,” the opposers of Chassidus, but of the other factions of Chassidim themselves!
Under the weight of this unparalleled and undeserved hostility, Rebbe Nachman’s students felt quite heavy and rightfully so. That was all until their first Shabbat Chanukah in Breslov with the Rebbe.

There were three times a year that Rebbe Nachman exhorted his disciples to be with him, without exception. These established times were Rosh HaShana, Shavuot, and Shabbat Chanukah. When the disciples of Rebbe Nachman arrived in Breslov for Shabbat Chanukah, they opened up to their Rebbe about the harsh and unfair criticism being directed towards them. The main source of torment was from a fellow Jew in the nearby town of Nemirov who had been falsely persecuting the Breslover Chassidim.

Rebbe Nachman responded immediately, as he was known to do, by delivering an ingenious lesson dealing with the specific challenges brought up by his students, intricately weaving their vexation and concerns into a novel and comprehensive Torah lesson about life (Likutey Moharan 8). Rebbe Nachman told his Chassidim afterwards, “Should you be asked what you accomplished here in Breslov, tell them Ruach!” (Chayei Moharan 130)

What is so powerful about, “ruach,” breath, that it should have allayed the troubles of Rebbe Nachman’s faithful students? What is it about “ruach” that should allow us 210 years later to deal with the frenetic challenges of modern life? The answer can be found in this week’s Parashah, Parashat Va’eira.

When HaShem asked Moshe Rabbeinu to take the Jewish People out of Mitzrayim, he responded, “But they will not listen to me.” After tremendous encouragement, Moshe entered the heart of exile to tell his suffering brethren that redemption was coming. The Torah states that they could not hear Moshe because of “kotzer ruach,” shortness of breath. Not that Moshe’s message was not transformative or novel. They simply could not make out what Moshe was saying because they could not catch their breath.

The Zohar compares the Tzaddik, the spiritual master of the generation, to Shabbat. Shabbat is a time of deep, restorative rest. This is a quality of rest that is not offered by the modern world. However, to access the tranquility and ecstasy of Shabbat is not as simple as turning off your phone and television. It first requires a deep breath.
Paroh and the Mitzrim worked the Jews to the pulp and, as a result, they could not hear the answer to their lifelong distress.
So too, modern life and society have relegated the only message of true comfort completely inaudible to the modern Jewish ear, secular and religious alike.
And herein lies the the powerful message of Rebbe Nachman. What is this great spiritual master offering in Breslov that is practically non-existent elsewhere?
The ability to take a deep breath.

And with this breath alone, Rebbe Nachman explains that one draws life force into each and everyone of his or her lackings. It is no surprise then that modern psychology utilizes deep breathing, especially with its most acutely pained clients, prior to any type of therapeutic intervention. Without this deep breath, they “cannot hear” the wisdom or advice needed to come out of their challenges.

But rather than give a temporary panacea to deep rooted suffering, Rebbe Nachman teaches us how to have the ability to breath deeply always. We do this through his innovative approach to daily secluded meditation, known as Hitbodedut. We do this through his unprecedented wisdom and comprehensive advice given on every situation and challenge that we come across in our lives. We do this through the echoes of his roar of unmitigated hope in the face of all trials and tribulations.
Rebbe Nachman teaches one how to breath. And in doing so, we can finally hear our inner voice telling us what it has been silently screaming all along.

And if you are like me, and like any of the students of Rebbe Nachman before me, than you have also faced your own share of unwarranted criticism and cynicism. Whether these attacks levied against you are primarily external or even deeply internal, there is only one real way to respond to questions about the legitimacy and potency of Breslov Chassidus and its Rebbe.

/parashas-vayechi-dec-17th-18th-2021/: (Dedicated to my father for his Refua Shlema, Avraham Ben Sarah Esther, and an Aliyah of the Neshama for Zecharia Yosef Yisrael Ben Moshe Yitzhak)

As we come to our conclusion of the first book of the Torah, something quite beautiful is coming into focus. To truly grasp this beauty, we must first remember a principle transmitted by our Sages. The unfolding of spiritual reality, paralleled exactly by the unfolding of physical reality, hinges on a unique phenomenon known as “The end is wedged in the beginning.” This foundational principle is teaching us that the end of any process must faithfully reflect the original purpose for the process itself.

For example, when an architect is hired to create a world-class structure, he begins by meditating on the purpose of the structure. Only then does he begin to formulate ideas which could give birth to that desired goal. Once the idea has been concretized, then the architect draws up a blueprint. From there, construction workers are hired to build this structure from the ground up.

From the beginning of construction until the end, the original purpose of the structure becomes obscured by the intensive labor taking place. Only once the building is finalized does the structure actually shine with the original purpose and vision for which it was created.

So too, our world is in a delicate period in which the purpose of its being created is deeply obscured. In fact, according to Rebbe Nachman, we are reaching a new point in history where the true meaning of our lives is doubly concealed from us. But through utilizing the principle of “The end is wedged in the beginning”, we can still make out the ultimate destination of this challenging and unique time period.

The Torah began with “In the beginning, HaShem created the spiritual and physical universe”. In the final chapter of the first book of the Torah, Parshat Vayechi, we learn about the conclusion of the lives of Yaakov Avinu and his beloved son Yosef.
What’s the inherent connection between HaShem originally creating time and space, and the ultimate recounting of the final moments of the lives of Yaakov and Yosef?
The answer is that HaShem created the world for one purpose alone. That purpose was not to become wealthy or famous. It was not to chase after selfish motives or to embrace nihilism.
The purpose of everything was to cultivate a relationship between a son and his father.

Our Sages teach, “One is obligated to say that the whole world was created just for me”. Rebbe Nachman adds that while its true that the world was created just for me, it is only in order that I should find Him.

Growing up, my father and I spent a lot of time together. We shared a love of sports and classic rock. My father was good at sports. I was bad at them. My father was a Paul McCartney fan. I was a John Lennon fan. My father liked The Who. I was obsessed with Led Zeppelin. One song that we both loved however is called “Father and Son” by Cat Stevens.

“I was once like you are now, and I know that it’s not easy. You’re still young. That’s your fault. There’s so much you have to go through. All the times that I’ve cried, keeping all the things I knew inside. Now there’s a way, and I know, I have to go away.”

The dynamic of father and son is so poignant and yet so complicated. Its full of love, but at times indescribably painful. Their personal journey’s leave them estranged at periods, yet they remain inextricably connected. The inner yearnings of both father and son are inherently good, but the events of their lives fuddle those innate desires.

However, just as the purpose of the world can only be found at the end of it, so too the true relationship of father and son can only be fully appreciated at the end. The relationship of Yaakov and his son Yosef reflects the unique relationship HaShem has with each of us.

It begins with a special love. That love prompts the father to send his son away to check on “his brothers”. Along the way, he is sold and enslaved, alienated from his family and society. Through the memory of his father and the courage of his conviction alone, he makes it out alive. Along the way, he finds genuine healing and eternal strength for all his father’s children. Afterwards, father and son finally reunite in an emotional, teary eyed embrace. And the purpose of their personal journeys and painful periods of separation finally weave into one exquisite tapestry. A tapestry that testifies to the ultimate truth. That the son and father are really one, and therefore had never left each other to begin with.

I bless each of us to have the courage, the patience, and the resilience to see this thing through till the end. To continue searching for Him and His love for you even when the events of your lives point to the contrary. To keep fighting until father and son are shown to be one.

There is a famous saying that frequented the lips of my Rebbe, Rav Walkin Ztl, as tears would well up in his eyes, “The final chapter has yet to be written!” With HaShem’s help, we should see it written very soon. Until then, hold on.
Emunah at the Heart of Imperfection
One of the foundational concepts that can be learned from the lives of our Avos and Imos is the concept of emunah- emunah that is forged from within imperfection and difficulty and the

daily trials of what it means to be a human being in Olam Ha’zeh where the light of spirituality can so often feel imperceptible. Avraham endures ten tests. Yitzchak is nearly killed by his father. Yaakov lives for years in the home of his father-in-law who takes every opportunity to exploit him. Yehudah is intimate with Tamar who poses as a prostitute. The list continues. The lives of our forebearers were not lives of perfection. Living a G-dly life is not equated to living a perfect life. Living a G-dly life is about having emunah that one’s imperfect life is perfectly placed within Hashem’s plan, as the title of Rabbi Elimelech Goldberg’s book on helping kids with cancer –
A Perfect G-d Created an Imperfect World Perfectly

At the core of their experiences is the awareness that Hashem is right there, as is most potently expressed in last week’s parashah when Yosef tells his brothers after revealing himself to them, “So now it was not you who sent me here, but G-d” (45:8).
Rebbe Nachman offers us an insight into living with emunah. Rebbe Nachman teaches in the 4th Torah in sefer Likutey Maharan the concept of “borrowing from the future.”

The Rebbe references the Gemara is Pescahim 50a, which explains, “At present the blessing ‘Who is good and beneficent’ is recited over good, whereas, the ‘truthful Judge’ is recited over bad. But in the Future, it will be entirely ‘Who is good and beneficent.’ The holy name Y[K]V[K] amd the holy name Elo[k]im will be totally one” (p. 117, Volume 1, BRI printing).

In other words, a person can gaze at Olam Ha’zeh with eyes of Olam Ha’bah. By virtue of the fact that it will be good, a person can actually see things as good right now and learn to make a space inside for whatever difficulty has come his way.

The aforementioned point is the secret of emunah that has sustained the Jewish people throughout time. Perhaps, I cannot comprehend how whatever I am going through right now is good. However, by knowing that it will good, I can strengthen myself in the belief that it is also good right now. In so doing, I experience the imperfection of the human experience as precisely the place where emunah is grown.
/parashas-vayeishev-nov-26th-27th-2021/: For anyone who’s ever had a dream, he or she knows that the path to actualizing that dream is filled with obstacles and barriers. And while the dreamer is celebrated and romanticized, the truth is that a real dreamer must be a fearless warrior, willing to endure unfathomable hardships and resistance to achieve what he or she believes in.
In this week’s Parashah, we learn for the first time about the dreamer, Yosef, and his courageous journey towards fulfilling his lofty dreams.
Yosef was different. He was naive. He lacked awareness of what was considered “normative”. He acted in ways that weren’t socially acceptable.

And when Yosef began to verbalize his fantastical dreams, Yosef’s brothers found his grandiosity to be off-putting and even threatening. So much so that they began to harbor intense hatred and jealousy towards their youngest brother.
None of this stopped Yosef from chasing his dreams.
For despite the alienation and cruelty from the brothers whom he loved, Yosef understood that fulfillment of his dreams would be the fulfillment of the deepest yearning of his brothers as well.
But despite Yosef’s prodigious nature and pure intentions, in one moment, his entire life was turned upside down.
Not recognizing the consequences of being so thoroughly hated, he innocently chased his brothers into the field and before he knew it, was stripped of his garments and thrown into a pit.
His brothers deliberated the possibility of ending his life but
ultimately decided on selling him into the servitude of foreigners.
Yosef was sold four times before he began his period of slavery in Mitzrayim. There, he was falsely accused and sent into prisonfor over a decade.

Like many who have endured trauma, abuse, bullying, or suddenloss, what appeared at first to be the story of a promising young man with unlimited potential and a good heart, quickly unraveled into a nightmare of unspeakable proportions.
Yosef’s life prospects crumbled before his eyes and his family fell apart from the grief of a lost son.
Yet through all of this, there had been one missing piece. One glaring omission.
Where is HaShem in the midst of such horror and atrocity?

In one of the most powerful and poignant teaching of our Oral Torah, the Sages expounded “Yosef’s brothers were preoccupied with the selling of Yosef. Reuven was preoccupied with his sackcloth and fasting. Yaakov was preoccupied with hissackcloth and fasting. Yehuda was preoccupied with taking a woman (cohabiting with a prostitute), and HaShem was creating the light of the Mashiach.”

In what had appeared to be the complete disintegration of Yosef’s personal life and that of his family, HaShem had orchestrated this entire upheaval only in order to bring about the fulfillment of Yosef’s dreams. For in truth, they were His dreams as well.

At this time, six years ago, I was sitting by the light of my Chanukia, reading Tehillim, and crying over the intense emotional distress and relentless psychological turmoil I had experienced in the years since becoming Ba’al Teshuva.

was playing over and over in my mind, “It may appear that all your efforts and attempts are being rebuffed and rejected on High. It may be days, months, or even years that you feel HaShem simply isn’t interested in your service. In truth, all distancing is only for the sake of being brought close.”

With tears in my eyes, I begged HaShem, “I don’t even need you to help me. I’ve given up on that. I just need you to show me that Your are with me. And if I’m not who I believe I am, just tell me already, so I can stop fighting for this.”
That night, I had a dream.
I don’t feel comfortable yet to discuss the contents of that dream. But it became clear to me that HaShem was with me. And that my lifelong dreams weren’t mine alone, but they were His as well.
And just as Yosef before me, the seemingly catastrophic events in my life had served as the unlikely catalyst to begin the genuine fulfillment of my lifelong dreams.
Rebbe Nachman once stated that the greatness of HaShem lies in fact that He can take the most calamitous challenges of a person’s life, and transform them into his personal bliss.
With that message, I exhort all of my dear brothers and sisters reading this. No matter how bleak. No matter how hopeless. You must never give up.
For the greatness of HaShem is His ability to “turn all of your meniot into neimot.”
So dream and don’t give up.
Because maybe, just maybe, HaShem has the very same dream. Shabbat Shalom.
Hope at the Heart of Connection
In his shiur based on the teachings of the
, R’ Avi Fishoff, founder of TWiSTED Parenting – an
organization which helps parents with children experiencing “stage 4” psycho-emotional crisis – offers the following insight into this week’s parshah.
The Midrash explains that, on his own, it was not within Yosef’s capacity to overcome the test he encountered with Potifar’s wife. Therefore, as the gemara in
teaches, Yosef was able to transcend the test through seeing the image of his father’s face. The
the moment Yosef confronted the test, he felt totally alone. It was specifically within his aloneness that the yetzer hara (the proclivity within every Jew towards evil) overwhelmed Yosef

in a way that was above nature. It was only through seeing the image of his father, and therefore, feeling connected to his father that ultimately strengthened Yosef to overcome the test. The essential point is as follows: the capacity for a human to being to transcend the tests of his life is rooted in his ability to transform the emotional experience of aloneness, which so many of us often feel, to the experience of connectivity.

, accentuates that if Yosef imagined the face of his father and experienced thoughts that Yaakov did not love him, then the possibility of transforming aloneness to connection would have been lost and Yosef would have, G-d forbid, succumbed to the test. R’ Fishoff shared a connected teaching from the

which explains that Yaakov specifically gave Yosef the special multi-colored robe, not to show favoritism, but rather to strengthen his son. Yaakov understood that Yosef, as opposed to his brothers, was going to feel alone and marginalized. Therefore, Yaakov offered the robe to Yosef in order that Yosef should feel even within aloneness itself he was not alone. His father loved him. Therefore, when Yosef conjured the image of Yaakov within his inner world, he simultaneously opened himself up to the world of connectivity that energized his ability to subdue the yetzer hara.

I worked with a patient recently, a former Army Ranger, caught in the counterfeit experience of connection which substance abuse offers, who said to me that his most recent withdrawal left him feeling the most scared he has ever felt in his life. This was a man who experienced the horrors of combat over multiple deployments. Yet, while his traumas absolutely intensified the fear he felt, the existential aloneness is what shackled him to hopelessness. He had no father to think about. Therefore, the possibility of connection which rests at the center of healing, was closed off.

However, once in treatment, those shackles of hopelessnessbegan to break. Treatment offered this man the opportunity to connect with people who chose to care about his success – the first responders team, the social workers, the nurses, the doctor – all offered the possibility for relationship. EverydayI had the privilege of working with him, I saw his eyes shine with new hope.

Herein lies the point – every moment we share with another human being can offer that person the possibility of connectivity. That is to say, the same way Yosef thought of his father and felt connected to his father and was, therefore, able to overcome his test, so too are we able to be the “Yaakov” to somebody else’s “Yosef.” At the heart of every encounter lies the opportunity to help a person transform the experience of aloneness to the experience of relationship. It is within the experience of connection itself which rejuvenates one’s ability to taste even the hope that was at one time impossible.
/parashas-vayeitzei-nov-12th-13th-2021/: I once had a student who suffered from tremendous internal doubts about his faith. He rarely spoke in class and it was fairly difficult to gauge what was going on inside of him. One day, he stopped showing up entirely.

I tried reaching out to him over the course of a few weeks to see how he was doing, but he didn’t pick up his phone or respond to my messages. I continued to pray for him every day, hoping that he would find whatever it was that he was looking for.
Purim was right around the corner, and he was still no where to be found. However, when my students put together a Purim party, he showed up unexpectedly.
He approached me with a huge smile on his face and thanked me deeply. I never saw him smile like that.

He proceeded to open up to me for the first time about his lifelong difficulties with believing in HaShem, as well as his more recent challenges in connecting to the teachings of Rebbe Nachman. He told me that he had essentially given up on Judaism and this was the real reason why he stopped coming to class.

However, he felt bad about the fact that the one plan of action I advocated so strongly for, he could never push himself to do. Finally, he told me that before he gives up on HaShem completely, he felt it was only fair to follow through with Rebbe Nachman’s main piece of advice.
No distraction. No interruption. 60 consecutive minutes of secluded personal conversation with the Creator of the universe, like He is your best friend (Likutey Moharan Tinyana, 25).

My student explained that during the first 45 minutes, he felt absolutely nothing. However, in the last fifteen minutes, he started to feel an ever increasing wave of peacefulness and tranquility come over him. Finally, when he reached the 60 minute mark, he stated with tremendous enthusiasm, “For the first time in my life, I saw G-d!”
What makes Hitbodedut the ultimate mechanism for experiencing the awesome reality of HaShem?
Why did Rebbe Nachman so frequently “pound the table” for this unique universal practice?
In this week’s Torah portion, “VaYeitzi”, we find the answer.

As Yaakov Avinu was departing from his home, looking to establish his personal path in spirituality, he decided to engage in the unique practice passed down by his father and grandfather in theexact place that they had practiced it. Following a long journey to Beit El, Yaakov had his first documented session of Hitbodedut.
Following a life changing, out of body experience, the Torah states that Yaakov entered a state of rapture and exclaimed, “HaShem is right here, and I didn’t know it!”.
In a remarkable lesson in Likutey Moharan, Rebbe Nachman describes the mechanics of Hitbodedut and the source of its tremendous efficacy.

When a Jew secludes himself from society and it’s external trappings, while concurrently speaking to HaShem for an extended and uninterrupted period of time, he or she experiences a psycho spiritual state of ego-dissolution (Likutey Moharan, 52).

One’s lower self, the ego, which is comprised of the powerful pursuit for temporary pleasure, the desire for external admiration, and fear of extraneous forces, melts away entirely. The “Neshama”, one’s higher, innermost self, rises to the forefront, knocking one into a powerful state of G-d consciousness previously unexperienced.

This powerful state of self nullification known as “Bitul”, is the hallmark of the Baal Shem Tov’s novel spiritual path known as Chassidut. The Baal Shem Tov’s great grandson, Rebbe Nachman, states matter of factly that the only way to reach this genuine state of “Bitul”, is through Hitbodedut.
My student, as his ancestor Yaakov before him, came to the same conclusion, “How awesome is this place! This is nothing other than the House of HaShem. This is the gate to Shamayim!”

Rebbe Nachman teaches that Avraham Avinu saw Hitbodedut as a “mountain”, a challenging terrain for the courageous minority to climb. Yitzhak Avinu saw Hitbodedut as a “field”, less arduous and more accessible, but still off-limits to the majority. Yaakov Avinu however, saw Hitbodedut as a “home”, the ultimate safe space and place of inner comfort, one needed and desired equally by all. Once Hitbodedut becomes a universal practice of humanity, Jew and non-Jew alike, Rebbe Nachman states that we will be privy to the Redemption and coming of Mashiach (Likutey Moharan, 10).
I encourage everyone to take this advice to heart and find one hour during Shabbat to pour out your heart to HaShem in your own words, like He is your best friend, and bring that state of
Geula closer. With this you will begin to find the home you always yearned for but never truly believed existed.
As HaShem himself states in His Torah, “Build Me a home and I will dwell in them”.
That “home” is Hitbodedut and that dwelling space is not outside of you, it’s within you.
“That “home” is Hitbodedut and that dwelling space is not outside of you, it’s within you.”

He writes, “There is no doubt that in truth, apart from the objective that is derived from the straightforward meaning of those stories about moral behavior like all other historical accounts, there must also be a powerfully [deep] objective in the stories, to hint at great secrets and the ideas related to all the true branches of wisdom” (p. 158, from R’ Avinoam Fraenkel’s translation).

The aforementioned point roots us in a principle we discussed in last week’s article: while the basic text is offering us insight into the stories of our Avos and Immos, a deeper reading yields insight into the dynamics that play out within our own inner worlds. Rabbi Ergas writes further, “In the end, with the entire Torah, the text talks in terms of the lower worlds [this physical world], but it hints at the supernal worlds…” (p. 164).
As we mentioned last week based on a conversation I had with my teacher, Rabbi Gerzi, “the Ari HaKodesh in

, Perek Aleph relates that the four spiritual universes – Atzilus, Beriah, Yetzirah, and Asiah – exist not only in the cosmic sense as a reality outside of the self, but also in a psychological sense that exist within the self” (London, “The Chumash Within”). Therefore, if the text of the Torah “hints at the supernal worlds” and our tzaddikim teach that the supernal worlds also exist as modes of consciousness, then we can understand that the text of the Torah is inviting us to experience our Avos and Immos, not just as personalities, but as psychological modes of being as well.

With the above introduction in mind, let us now move inwards, towards the ‘Leah’ that exists at the core of our human experience. Rabbi Y.Y. Jacobson, in his article, “Do You Know Who You Married?,” conveys the following point in regards to marriage: “‘Leah’, a name that literally means “one who is weary”, represents those elements in our spouse that are more complicated, perplexing and disturbing. Leah, the weak-eyed sister, weakened from tears and anxiety, embodies our continuous and exhausting struggle with the dark demons and ugly impulses in our lives.”
While Rabbi Jacobson is referring to the ‘Leah’ within one’s spouse, I think it is clear that the concept of ‘Leah’ exists also within ourselves.
The Torah characterizes Leah’s eyes as tender. Our eyes are tender as well. We also cannot stop crying.
Rashi explains that the reason Leah could not stop crying was because “she was under the impression that she was destined to ascend to the lot of Esau” (p. 322, Artscroll translation).

Leah was not married to Esav, and yet, the fear of the possibility was enough to have the Torah define Leah by her wearied, crying eyes. Is that not the condition of anxiety today – running away from something that is not even there?
In the midst of our tears, Rebbe Nachman whispers to us a secret: “Close your eyes,” he says. In Torah 65 of sefer

, Rebbe Nachman explains that when a person is undergoing suffering, he has to close his eyes completely from the experience of being in this world. He has to close off all external stimuli and soften into the darkness of the inner world. It is precisely that darkness which provides the possibility to see with the strong, inner eye – the eye that perceives that truly everything is from Hashem and everything Hashem does is to invite us into a more profound experience of goodness. The concealment of Hashem’s light we experience with eyes open becomes the revelation of Hashem’s light with eyes closed. Then, when we gaze at the aspect of ourselves called ‘Leah’, all the darker parts of ourselves shine with the possibility of renewed healing.

In this week’s parsha we read about Yaakov venturing out on his own. Taking his journey to find his wife, unable to return home where his bloodthirsty, twin brother Esav is ready to kill him for taking Issac’s blessing. There are many perplexing questions here. Firstly, the famous question, how could Yaakov, the tzaddik, the “ish taam”, man of simplicity do such a thing? After all, when we think of a man of holy simplicity, we would assume he’s someone who’s straightforward, never lying or attempting clever tricks. Another question that’s perplexed me is, why go through any of this in the first place? Why slight your brother and trick your father to end up impoverished and on the run when it was your blessing to receive in the first place. Why not just come up to Isaac and say, “Esav has sold me his birthright, he has no rights to it now. I am now considered your firstborn, please bless me as such.” In fact, that’s exactly the approach I’d expect from an “ish taam”, just being forthright and simple about the truth. Why go through all this?

Well, a deeper “truth” may lie in Rav Nachman’s teachings to help shed some light on the perplexing behavior of our holy forefather. Rav Nachman explains there are different levels of truth. In our society, we were raised to believe that there’s the truth, and then there’s a lie.
But according to chasidut, there are lies, then truths, then different ascending levels of higher truths. For example, when Rabbi Natan (Rabenu’s main student), was finally

offered his dream job of being chief Rabbi of his town, he came to Rav Nachman for advice on whether he should take the position. Rav Nachman said, “it’s an amazing position, you’re perfectly suited for it, there’s no better fit than you, and the entire community will benefit immeasurably from you being rabbi.” This made Rabbi Natan very happy to hear, as he held Rabenu’s advice in very high regard. But then Rabbi Natan thought to himself, “Wait, Rabbi Nachman taught me that there’s the truth, then there’s the “truth of truths”.

Rabbi Natan asked Rabbi Nachman “is that the truth?” Rabeinu responded “Yes”. Then he followed up with, “But is it the truth of truths?” Rabeinu responded: “No, the truth of truths is you will gain much more learning by me and working on writing and spreading my teachings.”

Rabbi Natan listened to Rabbi Nachman, despite the fact that it meant walking away from his longtime dreams and desires for himself. And we’re glad he did today. Because Rabbi Nachman was right. Had he taken that position he would not have spread the teachings that have a massive global effect we see today. Millions of people, Jews and non-Jews alike benefit immeasurably from these teachings for over two centuries.

These teachings have brought people peace, emuna, tshuva, closeness with God, better relationships, and have even pulled people out of the brink of suicide. There’s the truth, then there’s the truth of truths. And what does Rabbi Nachman say is the highest level of truth? – Shalom, aka peace. It’s also one of HaShem’s names. It doesn’t just mean when there’s no war. It refers to the Kabbalistic expression of Godliness where HaShem is able to make two paradoxical opposing forces in harmony with each other.

This means (going contrary to what many people would think), bending the truth for the sake of peace would technically be a higher truth than being outright and honest if it means I am hurting someone or making a big fight. Because there’s the truth and then there’s the truth of truths. The truth is that it was Yaakov’s birthright, he can demand it. But that means coming to his father and telling him his dear firstborn son Esav, a relationship Isaac treasures, sold his firstborn status for some soup. “That’s how much Esav values your blessing and being your firstborn.” Perhaps this would have broken Issac’s heart. But it’s the truth?! Yes, but then there’s the truth of truths, which is peace. Yaakov went against his simple nature to do something very out of character and send him running for his life but he stuck to the truth of truths.

When Leah was put in Rachel’s place at her wedding, she was quiet. But wasn’t this supposed to be her husband? She had every right to speak up, this was a terrible injustice. That’s the truth. But the truth of truths is that it’s better to remain quiet than to embarrass her sister. And thank HaShem for Rachel remaining quiet, because Leah marries Yaakov and has Yehuda, from whom comes Moshiach. The geula of the world could rest on just one person – one time deciding to forgo the truth and seek out Shalom – the truth of truths, even if it means letting go of what we think we are owed, because HaShem wants to give us so much more.
/parashas-vayigash-dec10th-11th-2021/: In Parashat Vayigash, an epic confrontation takes place between two of the most compelling figures in the Torah. Yehuda, the courageous and unquestioned leader of the Children of Yaakov, aggressively approaches Yosef, the charismatic and dynamic younger brother who’s life had inexplicably transformed from that of intense personal suffering and servitude to that of unparalleled spiritual mastery and universal influence.

The most gripping part of this showdown is that Yehuda does not actually know he is speaking to Yosef, for he had not seen his younger brother in 17 years. Instead, Yehuda thought he was speaking to the harsh and unsympathetic viceroy of a foreign kingdom. At the apex of Yehuda’s frustration, he even told Yosef he was like “Pharaoh,” the ruthless militant leader of an unjust society.
At the very same time, Yosef knew exactly who he was speaking to. As the Torah states regarding this unusual dynamic, “Yosef recognized his brothers, but his brothers did not recognize him.”

Following the impassioned pleading of Yehuda, Yosef had to forcibly remove himself from the conversation. Due to the aching pain welling up in Yosef’s heart at the sight of his brother’s distress, Yosef excused himself to a private room where he proceeded to weep with great intensity. Afterwards, Yosef washed his face and came back out to continue his charade of indifference.

This mysterious back and forth is something our Sages go to great lengths to explain. However, it was not until my late Rabbi Aharon Walkin Ztl revealed something to me that made me realize the life changing depth of this entire interaction.

Based on a powerful Midrash, Rav Walkin explained that Yosef composed himself as a harsh and distant authority figure only to afford his brothers the opportunity to achieve genuine teshuva. Iwas an act rooted in the ultimate level of empathy. One in whichno one else would be capable of carrying out, as it required the

deepest level of maturity, emotional awareness, and genuine selflessness to perform. For without this external facade on the part of Yosef, his brothers would not have been able to rectify the egregious error they made two decades earlier in exiling Yosef from his own home and estranging him from the only family he ever knew.
The fundamental point Rav Walkin added to this Midrash, and one in which Rebbe Nachman similarly expounds on as well, is that just as Yosef is the archetypal “Tzaddik Yesod Olam,” the

central figure on whom the entire world stands, he is only a mere reflection and window into the ultimate “Tzaddik Yesod Olam,” HaShem himself. That is to say, that the entire drama between Yosef and his brothers is really an exact parallel to the drama currently unfolding between HaShem and us.

Therefore, the painful experiences we have all endured in our lives, the private grudges we have developed and continue to harbor, and the heartfelt pleading we have since engaged in withHaShem, are all reflected by Yehuda approaching Yosef.

HaShem’s seeming “indifference” to our plight is really nothing other than the rich soil from which our individual heroism will ultimately blossom. HaShem’s ability to withhold his true intentions and feelings, are paradoxically His greatest compassion.
But be sure of this. Just as Yehuda before us, if we refuse to give up and continuously approach Him, one day soon we will also get to hear the truth.
And in the meantime, while we are trying to muster up the courage to continue fighting, remember and meditate deeply on this point.
While you are in distress, HaShem is not just listening. He is also crying with you.
This is actually the greatest comfort of all.

/parashas-vayishlach-nov-19th-20th-2021/: The most crippling part of struggle, both physical and psychological, is the deep rooted belief that you and I are victims. Each painful life experience furthers incapacitates us, reinforcing the core belief of victimhood. Over the course of time, we subconsciously build up this invisible, larger than life, state-of-the-art prison of helplessness from which most find it impossible to ever truly escape.

The main lesson which HaShem is desperately and repeatedly trying to impart to His beloved children throughout the entire Torah is “cheirut“, freedom. It’s a Mitzvah from the Torah to remember each and every day, “I am HaShem, your G-d, that took you out of slavery”. The depth of this Mitzvah is not to emphasize the collective, historical servitude of the Jewish people in Egypt from which we were ultimately released.
Instead, it is a deeply personal divine command to be fiercely and unapologetically empowered.
That at every waking moment of your life, regardless of the dark and painful places you have been to, you are free!
Rebbe Nachman teaches that the greatest spiritual impurity is not moral or even religious, it’s despair itself.

Why did Rebbe Nachman scream in a loud voice “Ein Shum Yeush B’Olam Klal”, there is no such thing as despair in the world at all? He should have just said it or even whispered it. Rebbe Nachman needed to scream it, because despair is a lie. So he screamed it.
Yes, it’s a juicy lie. Yes, it’s a gripping lie. Despair enthralls and captivates us. But nonetheless, it’s still a lie. And a lie can mamash kill you. It almost killed me.

Growing up with numerous debilitating episodes of depression and anxiety, I had become accustomed to feeling powerless. It lead to countless therapists, numerous psychiatrists, and endless experimentation with psychotropic medications. The side effects of these medications and psychiatric interventions have, to this very day, sapped me of my physical energy and mental clarity. In fact, those side effects put me into a greater state of despair than the original psychological distress itself!
But then HaShem whispered, you’re not a slave anymore. And then the Sages stated matter of factly that giving up is forbidden. And finally Rebbe Nachman screamed, despair doesn’t even exist!
My inner voice of disempowerment began to truly change when I read this week’s Parsha, Vayishlach, for the first time.

Yaakov struggles interpersonally with his brother Esav his entire life, from the womb until the grave. Rebbe Nachman teaches that Yaakov represents the Jew’s capacity for joy whereas Esav is the embodiment of sadness. Their lifelong struggle is actually reflective of our intrapersonal battle for happiness.
The culmination of this war is when Esav physically throws Yaakov down to the ground and in the process threatens to end his very existence. At the moment that all hope appears
utterly lost, Yaakov flips Esav into submission, causing Esav to beg Yaakov to release him.
What took place next is what stunned me and ultimately changed me.
Yaakov refuses to let Esav go.
“I won’t release you until you bless me,” Yaakov roared.
Can you imagine? Your darkest skeleton in your closet. Your greatest trauma. Your deepest fear. Your most acute pain. They come to you and say “You win, let me go”.
How much would you pay to release him? How much would you give up to finally let him go?
But Yaakov is teaching the most essential of all lessons.
Our problems are not to cripple us until we have the merit to move beyond the pain.
Our darkness is to be cast into submission and then transformed into light itself. Our darkness is meant to “bless us”.

Rebbe Nachman states that there is a higher form of joy than happiness itself. It’s when one transforms his own feelings of sadness into joy itself. This, the Tzaddik teaches us, is the greatest bliss.
To go from Yaakov, meaning “the heel”, to Yisrael, “the one who fights with the Divine” and emerges victorious.
It’s this paradigm shift that encouraged me to add the name Yisrael to the beautiful name my parents gave me at birth, and to forge forward with conviction and courage.
I’m not a slave. I’m free.
I love you and thank you for listening to me.
on this week’s parashah, Rav Itche Meir Morgenstern describes one of the foundational points in avodas Hashem. He explains, “But the path of Esav, the

I wanted to teach my patients that they did not need to be subservient to the natural ebbs and flows of their inner worlds. They could sing and dance. Then, with a sense of menuchas hanefesh as R’ Itche Meir suggests, go one foot in front of the other towards Hashem, only to find that He is with us every step of the way.

Crossing the Narrow Bridge
Rabbi David Yisrael Kalmus
“These are the children of Yitzhak, the son of Avraham. Avraham gave birth to Yitzhak.
These are the opening words of Parshat Toldot, and they contain a very profound secret.

Often in life, we feel alone. Troubled by the lack of apparent good in in our personal lives and chaos in the world at large, we can’t help but wonder, “Is there really a G-d watching over us?” And even if there is, “Does He actually care about me?”

Adding to the difficulty is the Torah’s novel assertion and foundational principle that everything that takes place in one’s life is nothing other than the constant unfolding and revelation of the Infinite Oneness of HaShem.

The preeminent Italian Kabbalist, Moshe Chaim Luzzato, states in his classic work Da’at Tevunot, that the purpose and destination of our lives is to experience the ecstasy of recognizing the absolute Unity of HaShem permeating all of reality and history.
Rebbe Nachman says that one can actually achieve this in their lifetime, and in doing so, experience a taste of “The World to Come” while still in this world (Likutey Moharan, 4).
It all sounds beautiful, and far be it from me to deny the insights of our spiritual masters, but why does life so often point to the contrary?
Depression, anxiety, anger, confusion, illness, abuse, trauma. That’s only what’s going on inside me. In society, there is hatred, jealousy, manipulation, oppression, apartheid, genocide.
How can one manage to recognize Unity in such brokenness?
Comes the Torah to teach us, “Avraham gave birth to Yitzhak.”
In Kabbalah, Avraham represents the profound experience of the Infinite light of HaShem permeating all of physical reality, without any concealments or obstructions.
This was Avraham’s spiritual essence and this elevated state of consciousness is what Avraham brought to the world.
Yitzhak, on the other hand, represents the complete opposite. Not the wondrous experience of revelation, but the overwhelming concealment of this Infinite light.

Yitzhak’s time was oft spent in complete solitude, engaged in the laborious work of excavating wells which his father had previously dug up. Yitzhak was kicked out from the only place he had achieved sustained success in adulthood. He lost his eye sight in his elder years and saw his favorite child take a turn for the worst prior to his passing. In the end, Yitzhak’s life was not one of self-development, but one of self-sacrifice.
Therefore, the Torah is teaching us a paradigm shift of the highest order.
It is HaShem’s Infinite love itself, called “Avraham”, that gives birth to the very concealment of that love, “Yitzhak”.
Put simply, when a father loves his child, he teaches him or her how to walk. Hand in hand they embrace and traverse across the floor.
But when he loves his child even more, he lets go. In doing so, his child can learn to walk on his or her own, this being the greatest expression of love.

The child doesn’t feel this way because he or she is not old enough to know their father’s real intentions. They also don’t possess enough awareness to appreciate the tremendous closeness of their father, even after having let go.

Therefore, HaShem gave us the Torah. So that even in the midst of our extended period of separation and lengthy exile, we can get a window into the true intentions that preceded our current fractured state.
That is, that “Avraham gave birth to Yitzhak.”
Love itself gave birth to distance and separation.
As a result, the bridge of life often feels incredibly narrow.
Notwithstanding, Rebbe Nachman stated empathically that the main thing is not to be afraid at all (Likutey Moharan Tinyana, 42).
Soon enough, Mashiach will reveal the truth.
Each personal journey provided unique tailor-made opportunities to cultivate growth and relationship that would be impossible without the possibility of challenge and adversity.

All of this is covertly reflected in Yitzhak’s name. Yitzhak is the future-form of the Hebrew word “tzchok”, laughter. Interestingly, Yitzhak means “he will laugh”. He doesn’t laugh now. At least not fully.
But when his eyes regain their pristine strength and he sees the eternal joy that his self-sacrifice gave birth to, Yitzhak and all of us crossing the very narrow bridge of life
will have “mouths that are filled with laughter”.
May it be truly soon in our days, amen.
“Each personal journey provided unique tailor-made opportunities to cultivate growth and relationship that would be impossible without the possibility of challenge and adversity. ” -Rabbi Kalmus
The Chumash Within
Aaron London, BSN, RN
R’ Aryeh Kaplan, in his remarkable work entitled
Chasidic Masters

, relates the following: “While the earlier Kabbalah tried to bring man into heaven, the main idea of Hasidism was to bring heaven into man” (4). Let us spend a few moments excavating the aforementioned point.

Perhaps, one of the most essential chiddushim that emerged from the school of the Baal Shem Tov was that the most esoteric concepts can be experienced on the level of one’s own personal avodas Hashem.
As one of my teachers shared with me recently, the Ari HaKodesh in
Shaar Gilgulim

, Perek Aleph relates that the four spiritual universes – Atzilus, Beriah, Yetzirah, and Asiah – exist not only in the cosmic sense as a reality outside of the self, but also in a psychological sense that exist within the self. Every Jewish individual, therefore, can experience his or her own inner Olam HaAtzilus, which is considered one of the highest dimensions that the Arizal revealed to us. This is an idea R’ Joey Rosenfeld also expands upon in shiur 15 (‘Each Person is His Own Universe’) in his series of shiurim entitled “Entering the Sea of Wisdom,” which are based on the teachings of Rav Yitzchak Meir Morgenstern from Yerushalyim.

In a similar vein, there is a principle that the narratives of the Chumash are not just historical events or the stories of our Forefathers or even moral lessons for time immemorial (even though these points are true). Rather, we can approach the stories of our Avos and the dynamics between them through a psychological lens.
With the above principle in mind, I want to suggest the following idea which I think yields a fascinating insight into the human experience.

Our sages teach us that that the Avos correspond to different middos. Avraham, as we know, corresponds to chesed, Yitzchak to gevurah, and Yaakov to emes/tiferes. Esav corresponds to the middah of Yitzchak, but in a corrupted way. Perhaps, we can say, Esav is the unhealthy expression of Yitzchak’s middah of gevurah, similar to Yishmael correlating to the unhealthy expression of Avraham’s middah of chesed.
Let us now look at an aspect of this week’s parsha through the psycho
emotional lens. The Torah explains, “Yitzchak loved Esav…” (Bereshis
25:28). Or, said differently, the middah of Yitzchak – gevurah, which

connotes the concept of judgement/boundaries/internality – loves the middah of Esav – the middah or proclivity towards the corrupted expressions of gevurah, such as criticism, meanness, hatred, etc. Rashi explains that the reason Esav returned home from the field exhausted was because he was worn out from murdering, which is perhaps the most severe manifestation of gevurah (Rashi on pasuk 29).

There is a subtle point I want to draw our attention towards and it is a point that I often see with the people I work with who suffer from substance abuse. It is a point that exists for most of us in varying intensities.

The idea of Yitzchak loving Esav is the idea of our own tendency towards “loving” habits and behaviors which are unhealthy. Not because there is something wrong with us, but rather we comfortably abide in those behaviors which have been reinforced over time. In a very real way, a person can feel more at home with the inner critical voice than the inner voice of self-forgiveness. Within one’s own space of internality (Yitzchak) he retains a negative bias towards the aspects of self rooted in Esav.

Nevertheless, there is the aspect of self which is called Yaakov. Yaakov, who corresponds to truth, balance, simplicity, and wisdom. And, within every Jewish individual, is this dynamic between Yaakov and Esav, between the part of ourselves which seeks the good and the part of ourselves which is biased towards negativity. Rebbe Nachman, in Torah Aleph of sefer
Likutey Moharan
, couches the dynamic of Yaakov and Esav within the concept of the yetzer tov and the yetzer hara.

Ultimately, Yaakov’s mission is to take ownership of the birthright. Rebbe Nachman elucidates in Torah Aleph that the birthright corresponds to the concept of chochmah/wisdom. In our context, the part of ourselves which is rooted in Yaakov must claim the “birthright” that lives within us. That is to say, the aspect of our spiritual consciousness called “Yaakov” must take ownership of the inner wisdom which exists at the core of who we are. That point of inner wisdom is where the true self abides in all its possibility of what healthy living can look like.

Perhaps, most profoundly, the “birthright” is constantly present within us. That inner point of wisdom which represents all the different facets of G dliness is never something outside of us. We just need the courage to take possession of that which has always been rightfully ours.
Gut Shabbos,
ALY
